# SE-2 completion — generated by `complete.py`, not hand-edited

## 1. Concurrency, and the guard that was not enough

The README refused to call the double-completion guard race-safe: it is a read-then-write with no transaction boundary, so two threads can both read "not yet completed" before either writes. That was correct, and here is the race.

| | threads | completions accepted | refused | exactly one won |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **with BEGIN IMMEDIATE + UNIQUE index** | 8 | **1** | 7 | **True** |
| without the index | 8 | 8 | 0 | False |

Eight threads released simultaneously off a barrier — without the barrier they run one after another and the test passes for the wrong reason. Refusal reasons: `duplicate completion for this pass`.

BEGIN IMMEDIATE takes the write lock at the START of the transaction so the read happens inside it; the UNIQUE index makes the invariant true in the schema, which is what holds against a client that forgets the transaction. The index is the half that matters: an application check protects code that goes through it, and a constraint protects against everything — including the migration script somebody runs at 2 a.m.

`pass_no` makes the constraint expressible at all. A reworked unit legitimately completes the same operation twice, so the unique key is (unit, seq, **pass**) rather than (unit, seq) — which is the same insight the rework bugs in pass 2 turned on.

## 2. Finite-capacity scheduling

`work_center.capacity` has existed since pass 1 and nothing read it. With 20 jobs across five work centres:

| plan | makespan | mean flow time | jobs late | total tardiness |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| infinite capacity (not a plan) | 1031 | 405 | 11 | 1866 |
| finite, FIFO | 2079 | 1058 | 16 | 12738 |
| finite, SPT | 2185 | 964 | 16 | 10377 |
| finite, EDD | 2146 | 973 | 17 | 10750 |
| finite, CR | 2185 | 964 | 17 | 10569 |

**Finite-capacity flow time is 2.6× the infinite-capacity plan**, and **62% of it is queue time**. That is the number an infinite-capacity planner promises away: a plant's lead time is dominated by waiting, not by cutting, and a plan that schedules three jobs onto one machine at 08:00 is not optimistic, it is arithmetically impossible.

**No rule dominates, which is the point of comparing them.** CR gives the best mean flow time (964) and EDD the best worst-case lateness. Choosing between them is choosing what the plant is judged on — average throughput or the one order that embarrasses you — and that is a business decision, not a technical one.

**The shift calendar is not decoration.** An 8-hour job started at 14:00 takes 16.3 elapsed hours — 2.04× — because it crosses a break and the end of second shift. Across the whole schedule the makespan inflates 1.66×.

## 3. Integration with DATA-1 and ML-1

**Equipment state gates operations:** 2 of 4 attempted starts refused.

| work centre | state | allowed | reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| WC-CUT | RUNNING | yes | — |
| WC-WELD | UNPLANNED_DOWN | **no** | WC-WELD is UNPLANNED_DOWN |
| WC-PAINT | PLANNED_STOP | **no** | WC-PAINT is PLANNED_STOP |
| WC-GRIND | UNKNOWN | yes | WC-GRIND state unknown -- allowed, but recorded |

**An unknown state fails OPEN and is recorded.** fail OPEN and record -- failing closed on a missing integration halts a plant because a message bus hiccupped. That is a deliberate choice with a cost — a genuinely down machine whose state never arrived will accept production — and the audit row is what makes the cost visible afterwards.

**ML-1 alarms become maintenance work orders:** 2 created, 1 suppressed as duplicates. A model that alarms every cycle would otherwise raise a work order every cycle, and maintenance would filter the feed within a week.

Both interfaces are narrow on purpose — a state provider and an alarm feed — because importing another project is what makes two systems impossible to deploy separately.

## 4. Electronic signatures and retention

6 records signed with a stated meaning, chain intact before tampering (True), broken and detected after (True)

| attempted violation | refused |
|---|---|
| sign with a free-text meaning | **yes** |
| alter the payload under a valid signature | **yes** |
| verify with the wrong key | **yes** |
| edit one row in place after the fact | **yes** |

**The audit chain is hash-linked**: each row carries the hash of its predecessor, so deleting or editing a row breaks every hash after it. Tamper detection: True, at row 3.

This is 21 CFR Part 11 *shaped* — signature meaning, signer identity, timestamp, and a link to the signed record — and it is **not** a compliant system. No identity provider, no password policy, no periodic review, no validation package. The gap is smaller than it was and it is still a gap.

## 5. Scale

200,000 genealogy edges, 15 MB, inserted at 40,672 rows/s.

| recall query | time |
|---|---|
| no index (full scan) | **51.6 ms** |
| index on lot_id | 0.06 ms (933× faster) |
| **covering index (lot_id, unit_id)** | **0.03 ms** (2.0× faster again) |

The README said the 0.7 ms figure was measured against 123 edges with warm caches and would change shape at millions of rows. It does: unindexed, the same query takes 52 ms.

The second step is the one worth knowing. A plain index on `lot_id` finds the rows and then reads each one from the table; a **covering** index on `(lot_id, unit_id)` contains the answer, so the query never touches the table at all. Query plan: `[(3, 0, 55, 'SEARCH consumption USING COVERING INDEX ix_cons_lot_unit (lot_id=?)')]`.

## 6. The operator terminal

`out/terminal.html`, 7 KB, self-contained. The dispatch list, the unit's routing with its completed operations, the materials to issue, and the disposition buttons. It renders the state and does not write — wiring it to `execution.py` needs a server, and a UI that silently no-ops would be worse than none.
